question: Silver-cheeked toadfish (Lagocephalus sceleratus) were first detected in Greece in 2005. Within a span of 23 years, the fish can now be found not only in Greek waters, but also in those of Italy and Spain. Recently, the damage they have caused to Greek fishers and their property has been extensive. They destroy their marketable catch and fishing gear, reducing their production capacity.

This directly affects the Greek fishing industry – a productive mainstay of the Greek economy. Coordinated European action is therefore required, as is compensation for fishers affected by silver-cheeked toadfish. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it provide compensation to fishers affected by silver-cheeked toadfish?
Will it take measures to address similar future risks?
In the context of drafting the new EU multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034, will it allocate additional resources to strengthen the resilience of the Greek fishing fleet?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. Member States can use the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) to fund targeted management actions and support fishers affected by non-indigenous species (NIS).

Greece has recently launched a relevant action, in a pilot phase, focusing on Lagocephalus and aiming to protect marine biodiversity through targeted fisheries management measures, scientific monitoring and remuneration to participating coastal fishers for targeted catching and landing. It is for the Member States to design and implement such measures within their national EMFAF programmes. 2.

The Commission announced a dedicated policy initiative within the Ocean Pact1 to address the issue of NIS. In addition, through collaboration and financial support to the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean, the EU has been supporting work on NIS through research programmes and establishment of a regional NIS observatory to enhance knowledge and share best practices in tackling NIS. 3.

For fisheries, the Commission proposal foresees a ring-fenced amount of EUR 2 billion for certain activities under the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), ensuring a minimum level of support for key CFP objectives, including sustainability, conservation of marine biological resources, innovation and the Common Market Organisation.

Member States will be able to complement this dedicated amount from the overall envelope of their national and regional partnership plans to address additional needs related to fisheries, aquaculture, coastal communities, the wider blue economy and the ocean.
1 Communication of the Commission on the European Ocean Pact, COM(2025) 281 of 5.6.2025.
